sources.citation: TransNewGuinea.org (Simon Greenhill), Chambri lexicon (404 items) drawn from Foley 1986, Foley 2005, 'SIL (1975) Summer Institute of Linguistics Language Survey of Chambri, 1975' and 'SIL (1977) Summer Institute of Linguistics Language Survey of Chambri, 1977'.https://transnewguinea.org/language/chambri
sources.note: Raw wordlist data only. The SIL 1977 forms carry stress marks (wɔ'bři 'hair', kʰa'ři 'head', 'wambušu 'nose', 'pan 'belly', ba'pokʰo 'small', hai'il 'fire', sɩnma'li 'sun', 'mwil 'moon') and correspond to Abbott 1985's Kilimbit list; the SIL 1975 and Foley lists are unmarked. Only page 1 of 9 was retrievable (pages 2-9 sit behind a JavaScript challenge).

sources.citation: Rosetta Project. 2010. Chambri Swadesh List (archive.org item rosettaproject_can_swadesh-1, CC-BY).https://archive.org/download/rosettaproject_can_swadesh-1/can.txt
sources.note: Merged Swadesh forms from several unnamed lists; a subset carries acute accents (esaló 'ashes', yambwí 'bird', karí 'head', kontsál 'fish', kamplénche 'cloud', nëmpárëkwenën 'girl'); no source attribution and no rule.

sources.citation: Foley, William A. 2005. Linguistic prehistory in the Sepik-Ramu basin. In Pawley, Attenborough, Golson & Hide (eds), Papuan Pasts (Pacific Linguistics 572), 109-144. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Nothing on stress: Chambri appears only in Lower Sepik comparative tables (numerals, pronouns, noun-class plurals) and in the remark that final nasal+stop clusters are simplified 'in all languages but Chambri'.

sources.citation: Abbott, Stan. 1985. Nor-Pondo lexicostatistical survey. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 22 (Pacific Linguistics A-63), 313-338. DOI 10.15144/PL-A63.313. Appendix B, pp. 329-338.
sources.note: No prose statement. A Chambri diagnostic list was elicited on 24 January 1977 at the Chambri Council center, Maprik (p. 319); in Appendix B the 'Kilimbit' column (Kilimbit is a Chambri village, p. 314) gives ~84 Chambri words in phonetic transcription with an apostrophe before the stressed syllable, e.g. 'ubo 'big', ba'pokho 'small', khe'li 'ear', 'namaŋkh 'foot', 'mwil 'moon', suvna'li 'sun', kam'plentše 'cloud', 'anamph 'bone', 'usim 'two'. Stress placement in these forms is mixed (initial, penult and final all occur); the convention is not explained and no rule is stated.
sources.venue: Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 22 (Pacific Linguistics A-63)

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. & John Z'graggen. 1975. The Sepik-Ramu phylum. In S.A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 731-763. Canberra: ANU. Section 2.11.3.3.1 'Pondo Family: CHAMBRI', pp. 754-757.
sources.note: Nothing for Chambri. The only published sketch of the language (based on 'a few hours with a Chambri informant in 1971') gives a phoneme inventory (p. 754), noun classes, numerals, pronouns and verb paradigms (pp. 754-757); no word on stress or accent. The phylum-wide feature list on p. 732 includes 'lack of complex suprasegmental systems', which is a Sepik-Ramu generalisation, not a Chambri statement.
sources.venue: New Guinea area languages and language study

sources.citation: n.a. n.d. [posted 2011]. Chambri Organised Phonology Data. Unpublished manuscript, 4 pp. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG / SIL International, SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 42248 (oai:sil.org:42248); draft posted 'as is' without peer review, issue date 2011-09-13.
sources.note: Says tone may be phonemic on the strength of one pair: waan level 'snake' vs. waan rising 'he is gone', the only example found; no tone system is proposed. Word stress apparently not phonemic.

tone.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Word stress does not appear to be phonemic. There is some evidence suggesting tone may be phonemic. The word waan said in a monotone is the word for 'snake', while waan said with a rising tone means 'he is gone'. This was the only example found.
tone.summary: Says tone may be phonemic on the strength of one pair: waan level 'snake' vs. waan rising 'he is gone', the only example found; no tone system is proposed. Word stress apparently not phonemic.
